title: What is the sum of the first hundred odd numbers?
description: A hundred L shaped layers make a grid of a hundred rows and a hundred columns, so the first hundred odd numbers add up to ten thousand. Keeko's doubt, that ten times more numbers gives ten times more in the sum, is broken.
teaching_notes: One idea: the sum of a hundred odd numbers is a hundred times a hundred, found by imagining the grid without drawing all of it. Watch for students who scale the sum by ten instead of squaring.

source: Now by imagining a similar picture, or by drawing it partial
video_script.why: The child imagines the grid for a hundred odd numbers, draws only part of it, and finds the sum as a hundred times a hundred.
video_script.substitution: The sum of the first n odd numbers is n times n, even when the grid is too big to draw.
video_script.anchor: a square grid with its first few layers drawn, a gap, and its last layer drawn, with the words 100 layers
video_script.wrong_answer: ten times more numbers gives ten times more in the sum
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko says ten times more numbers gives ten times more in the sum, so the answer is one thousand. A hundred layers make a grid of a hundred rows and a hundred columns, which grows both ways, and the doubt is struck.
video_script.payoff_line: The sum of the first one hundred odd numbers is ten thousand
hold_back: The sum of the first 100 odd numbers is 10000
never_show: ten times more numbers gives ten times more in the sum
maths_rules: the first 100 odd numbers make 100 layers of a square grid
100 layers make a 100 by 100 square grid
check: the pairs 1 + 199, 3 + 197 and so on each make 200, there are 50 pairs, and 50 x 200 = 10000
slip: 10 times as many numbers makes the sum 100 times as big, not 10 times as big
video_script.design: One idea: imagine the big grid and multiply the side by itself. Assumes the ten by ten case. Wrong idea: ten times more numbers gives ten times the sum. The part drawn grid stays on the board to the end.

narration: <bookmark mark='layers'/>Step one, imagine the grid. A hundred odd numbers make a hundred layers.

marks.mult: the multiplication 100 x 100 = 10000 is written under the grid

narration: <bookmark mark='mult'/>Step two, count the dots. A hundred rows with a hundred dots in each row have a hundred times a hundred dots. That is ten thousand.

beats.on_screen: Check, in pairs: 1 + 199 = 200, 3 + 197 = 200, and so on, 50 pairs, and 50 x 200 = 10000

narration: <bookmark mark='pairs'/>Step three, check by pairing. One and one hundred ninety nine make two hundred, and so do three and one hundred ninety seven.
<bookmark mark='fifty'/>There are fifty such pairs. Fifty times two hundred is ten thousand, as before.

beats.on_screen: Answer: The sum of the first 100 odd numbers is 10000
narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>The sum of the first one hundred odd numbers is ten thousand.

narration: <bookmark mark='hand'/>Keeko has raised a hand. Let us check the doubt and solve it.

beats.on_screen: Keeko's doubt in a bubble; a ten by ten grid beside a hundred by a hundred grid, each side marked ten times longer; the bubble is struck through

marks.both: the ten by ten grid and the hundred by hundred grid appear side by side with each side marked ten times longer

narration: <bookmark mark='doubt'/>Keeko thinks ten times more numbers gives ten times more in the sum.
<bookmark mark='both'/>But a hundred layers make a grid that is ten times longer and also ten times wider.
<bookmark mark='fix'/>The dots grow in both ways, so the sum is a hundred times bigger than before.
